chunks: Gyro/accelerometer applications. The question: What are its applications?
Accelerometers and gyroscopes let a device know how it is tilted, bumped, dropped, shaken or turned. The accelerometer reports gravity's direction and any pushes.
The gyroscope reports how fast the device is turning.
Phones, drones, cars and wearables use these two signals for rotating the screen, counting steps, stabilizing a camera, deploying airbags and more.
Your inner ear does the same two jobs. One part senses which way gravity pulls and when your head is pushed, like an accelerometer.
Another part senses when your head is turning, like a gyroscope. Your brain uses both to keep you balanced.
A device has no brain, so its software must turn the raw numbers into decisions: a screen flip, a step, an alarm.
The ear picture does not show that the device must pick its sensor settings for each job.
The magnitude removes the dependence on how the phone is held, the low-pass removes noise and impacts, and the minimum interval (about 250 milliseconds) rejects double counts.
Thresholds are adapted to the user's recent signal strength.
Accelerometer and gyroscope: sensors for pushes and gravity, and for rotation speed. Tilt: the angle of a device relative to gravity.
Free fall: falling with nothing holding you up, so an accelerometer reads about 0 g on every axis. Threshold: a trip level. The software acts only when the signal crosses it.
Image stabilization: canceling camera shake, using the gyroscope's measurement of the shake.
A phone in your pocket counts steps. Standing still, its accelerometer reads about 1 g in total, from gravity. Each footstep adds a small bump above that.
When the signal crosses a threshold, the software counts one step. It ignores any bump less than about 0. 25 seconds after the last one, since people do not step faster than that.
Walking at 2 steps per second, 10 seconds gives 20 counted peaks, so 20 steps. That is the whole idea.
"Accelerometers and gyros give a system its sense of motion and orientation.

Phones use them for screen rotation, step counting and image stabilisation, drones for attitude control at kilohertz rates, cars for airbag deployment and stability control, laptops and drives for free-fall protection, and factories for vibration-based predictive maintenance.
The applications differ in range, bandwidth and power: an airbag needs tens of g, a step counter microamps, a drone gyro low noise."
